title: Linear Boolean functions have degree at most one
statement: Let $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ be linear, meaning $f(x \oplus y) = f(x) \oplus f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \{0,1\}^n$, where $\oplus$ denotes componentwise XOR. Then $f$ has degree $\le 1$: its $\pm 1$ lift $(-1)^f$ has vanishing multiplicative derivatives of order two, so that for every base point $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ and every pair of directions $h_1, h_2 \in \{0,1\}^n$ the order-$2$ Gowers product of $(-1)^f$ over the combinatorial square $x + \operatorname{span}\{h_1, h_2\}$ equals $1$.
hypotheses_covered: f is a Boolean function on the n-dimensional hypercube
f is linear: f(x XOR y) = f(x) XOR f(y) for all x, y
replaced:
If $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear (i.e.\
$f(x \oplus y) = f(x) \oplus f(y)$ for all $x,y$), then $f$ has degree $\le 1$.
